text: Very friendly panel. They asked a lot about relocation and shift and whether I would sign the bond. No deep technical questions at all, mostly about my final year project.
Asked me to write SQL query for second highest salary and then kept asking about joins. Also asked about primary key vs unique key. My advice: revise SQL properly.
Total 15 minutes. Tell me about yourself, why TCS, relocation, and if I know what TCS does. They really want to hear that you are okay with any location.
70 percent of my interview was my project. They asked why I chose that database and made me explain the architecture on paper. Then normalization questions, 3NF specifically.
Panel drilled me on OOP for 20 minutes - overloading vs overriding, abstract class vs interface, then asked about ACID properties. Felt underprepared on theory.
Standard HR round. They asked what I would do if given a technology I do not know. Also asked about my Infosys Springboard certification, so do mention it.
Asked me to reverse a string and check palindrome in Java. Also difference between == and equals. Pretty basic, they mainly checked if I could explain my code.
HR asked about the service agreement and relocation straight away. Be very clear and do not hesitate on the bond question, they mark you down for that.
SQL heavy. Second highest salary, types of joins, then a question on when to use left join. They also asked me to pick one language and go deep.
Started from DBMS normalization and went into indexing. Asked why an index slows down inserts. I had read it but could not explain it well.
Almost entirely situational questions - missed deadline, team conflict, disagreeing with a senior. They want STAR format, that is it. Prepare 5 stories and you are set.
Very conversational. Asked where I see myself in 5 years and about my hobbies. Very important to look confident and smile, they judge communication a lot.
Every single round had two leadership principle questions. They dig for 4-5 follow ups on the same story - what exactly did YOU do, what was the metric. One story about ownership is not enough.
Two sum variant followed by a sliding window problem. They cared more about me stating complexity and edge cases than finishing the code. Always ask clarifying questions first.
Asked to design a URL shortener and then went very deep on how I generate the unique id and how I handle collisions. Also asked about caching and analytics. I underestimated this round.
No small talk, straight to the problem. They gave a hint only after I was stuck for a while. Very focused on optimal complexity, brute force was not accepted.
Rate limiter design. They expected me to compare token bucket vs sliding window and talk about distributed state. Tough round, prepare properly.
Reverse linked list and a tree question. The interviewer was helpful and wanted me to think aloud. They also asked one OS question about process vs thread.
Indexing and stack vs heap were asked. Also a debugging story from my project. Be ready to admit a bug you shipped, they like honesty there.
Flash sale inventory design. They kept pushing on how to avoid overselling. Concurrency and idempotency came up again and again.
C fundamentals and pointers. Nothing about frameworks. They also asked me why I was rejected somewhere before, so keep an honest answer ready.
Weakness, why should we hire you, and any questions for us. Having two good questions at the end changed the tone of the interview completely.
OOP four pillars, TCP vs UDP, and one binary search question. Mixed round, tested breadth over depth.
